d: Learn about vulnerability vectors from third-party assets.
h:
The following content covers various concepts and tactics to improve security and mitigate cheating in your Roblox games. It's highly recommended that all developers read through these to ensure that your games are secure and fair for all users. Check the sidebar for additional security topics.

Third-party assets from the Creator Store (Toolbox) are a common source of security risks, as they can contain malicious scripts called backdoors. These scripts give their creators unauthorized server-side access to your game, allowing them to manipulate its state, steal sensitive data, or disrupt the game for your players.

Backdoors are particularly dangerous because they often appear in otherwise legitimate-looking models. A seemingly innocent building or vehicle might contain a script that activates when certain conditions are met, such as when a specific player joins or a particular command is executed. When a model contains scripts, this is indicated in the Toolbox user interface before and during insertion.

Roblox moderates Models for malicious scripts both proactively and in response to reports, but this process is not guaranteed to remove all such scripts.

Protecting your game

The most effective defense against backdoors is sandboxing. When you insert a model, you should contain its scripts to prevent malicious code from reaching sensitive APIs or affecting systems outside the model itself.

  1. Set SandboxedInstance to Experimental on Workspace.
  2. In the Properties window, set the Sandboxed property of the model to true.
  3. Configure the Capabilities property to grant only the specific permissions the asset needs to function.

Note that during the beta, some features may not function as expected when Sandboxed, erroring with a message saying "...lacking Capability Unassigned". These will be fixed as Capabilities rolls out of beta.

Be especially cautious about granting Network, DataStore, AssetRequire, CapabilityControl, or LoadString capabilities to third-party assets unless you understand exactly why the asset needs them. These capabilities provide access to powerful systems that backdoors commonly exploit.

Before using any asset, carefully inspect its scripts. Pay particular attention to obfuscated or unusually complex code. Malicious actors often use deceptive techniques to hide harmful content, such as using whitespace to position malicious code off-screen when viewed in the studio editor. Consider favoring highly-rated community assets that have been vetted by other developers, though remember that popularity doesn't guarantee safety. For comprehensive guidance on configuring script restrictions, see Script Capabilities.

In the future, we plan to automatically sandbox all assets from the Creator Store with appropriate Capabilities.

kid.simple: Free models from the Creator Store (the Toolbox) can hide bad scripts called backdoors. A backdoor lets the person who made it secretly control your game, steal data, or ruin it for players. Even a normal-looking car or house can have one. This page shows how to box in a model's scripts so they can only do what they really need.
kid.analogy: Grabbing a free model is like taking a free toy from a stranger. Most are fine, but one might have a hidden microphone inside, so you check it and keep it in a room where it cannot hear much.
keyPoints: A backdoor is a hidden script that gives its creator secret server control of your game.
Backdoors often hide inside normal-looking models and may only switch on when a certain player joins or a command is typed.
The Toolbox shows when a model contains scripts, before and while you insert it.
Roblox moderation removes many bad models, but not all of them.
Best defense: sandbox it. Set Workspace's `SandboxedInstanceMode` to `Experimental`, set the model's `Sandboxed` property to true, then pick only the `Capabilities` it needs.
Be extra careful about giving a free model Network, DataStore, AssetRequire, CapabilityControl, or LoadString powers.
Read a model's scripts before using it. Watch for scrambled code or code pushed far off to the side with lots of spaces.
Popular, well-rated models are usually safer, but popularity does not guarantee safety.

terms.third-party asset: Something made by someone other than you, like a model from the Creator Store.
terms.Creator Store / Toolbox: The place in Studio where you can grab free models, images, sounds, and more made by others.
terms.backdoor: A sneaky script that lets its creator control your game without your permission.
terms.malicious: Made on purpose to cause harm.
terms.sandboxing: Putting something in a closed box with limited powers so it cannot affect the rest of your game.
terms.capability: One permission you can give a sandboxed model, like Audio or Physics.
terms.obfuscated: Made deliberately hard to read, often to hide what code really does.
terms.whitespace: Blank spaces and empty lines. Bad scripts can use lots of spaces to push code off the edge of the screen.

watchOut: Inserting a model without checking for scripts. Look for script icons and read every script inside.
Trusting a model just because it is popular. Still check it.
Giving a free model the Network or DataStore capability without knowing exactly why it needs it.
Missing hidden code. Scroll all the way right in long lines and be suspicious of unreadable code.
Panicking at "lacking Capability Unassigned" errors. During the beta some features do not work while sandboxed yet.
